items.followUp: Define mass/volume percentage and write its formula.

rubric.why: This identifies the quantities used to define volume/mass percentage.
rubric.description: Defines it as the volume of solute in 100 g of solution.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating the definition with the solute volume and solution mass.

rubric.why: The formula expresses the volume of solute as a percentage of the solution’s mass.
rubric.description: Gives the correct formula, with compatible units.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct formula and units.

modelAnswer: Volume/mass percentage is the volume of solute, in mL, present in 100 g of solution.
Volume/mass % = (volume of solute in mL ÷ mass of solution in g) × 100.

items.followUp: What does “like dissolves like” mean? Give one example.

rubric.why: The principle is based on the similarity of the solute’s and solvent’s polarity.
rubric.description: Explains that substances of similar polarity dissolve one another.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that polar substances dissolve in polar solvents and non-polar substances in non-polar solvents, or equivalent.

rubric.why: A correct example demonstrates the principle.
rubric.description: Gives a valid example of a solute dissolving in a like solvent.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a suitable example, such as salt dissolving in water or iodine dissolving in a non-polar solvent.

modelAnswer: “Like dissolves like” means that a solute dissolves best in a solvent with similar polarity: polar substances dissolve in polar solvents, and non-polar substances in non-polar solvents.
For example, ionic salt dissolves in polar water.

items.followUp: Why is potassium softer than calcium?

rubric.why: Magnesium contributes more valence electrons to the metallic bond than sodium does.
rubric.description: States that magnesium contributes two valence electrons, compared with sodium’s one.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this comparison or an equivalent statement about greater electron density in magnesium’s metallic bonding.

rubric.why: Stronger metallic bonding makes magnesium harder.
rubric.description: Links stronger metallic bonding in magnesium to its greater hardness.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct link between stronger metallic bonding and hardness.

modelAnswer: Magnesium contributes two valence electrons per atom to the metallic bond, while sodium contributes only one.
This gives magnesium stronger metallic bonding, so magnesium is harder than sodium.

items.followUp: Why is the first ionization energy of calcium higher than that of potassium?

rubric.why: The comparison is made between alkaline earth and alkali metals in the same period.
rubric.description: Identifies that the comparison is between elements in the same period (or outer shell).
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for noting that their outer electrons are in the same principal shell.

rubric.why: Greater effective nuclear attraction makes it harder to remove an electron from the alkaline earth metal.
rubric.description: Explains that the alkaline earth metal’s outer electron is held more strongly.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking greater nuclear charge and/or smaller atomic radius to stronger attraction and higher ionization energy.

modelAnswer: In the same period, an alkaline earth metal has a greater nuclear charge and a smaller atomic radius than the alkali metal before it.
Its outer electron is therefore held more strongly, so more energy is needed to remove it.

items.followUp: Why is the first ionization energy of aluminium greater than that of sodium?

rubric.why: Across a period, nuclear charge increases while the outer electrons remain in the same principal shell.
rubric.description: States that magnesium has a greater nuclear charge than sodium in the same period.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the relevant comparison of nuclear charge or effective nuclear attraction.

rubric.why: The stronger attraction to magnesium’s outer electron raises its ionization energy.
rubric.description: Concludes that magnesium’s outer electron is harder to remove, so its ionization energy is higher.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct explanation and conclusion.

modelAnswer: Magnesium has a greater nuclear charge and a smaller atomic radius than sodium, while their outer electrons are in the same principal shell.
The outer electron in magnesium is held more strongly, so more energy is needed to remove it; therefore, sodium’s ionization energy is lower.

items.followUp: Write the reactions of chlorine with cold and hot aqueous sodium hydroxide.

rubric.why: Chlorine disproportionates in cold, dilute sodium hydroxide to chloride and hypochlorite.
rubric.description: Gives the balanced reaction with cold aqueous sodium hydroxide.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct balanced equation and identifying the cold condition.

rubric.why: In hot, concentrated sodium hydroxide, chlorine forms chloride and chlorate.
rubric.description: Gives the balanced reaction with hot aqueous sodium hydroxide.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct balanced equation and identifying the hot condition.

modelAnswer: Cold, dilute solution: Cl₂ + 2NaOH → NaCl + NaClO + H₂O
Hot, concentrated solution: 3Cl₂ + 6NaOH → 5NaCl + NaClO₃ + 3H₂O

items.followUp: Write any five postulates of Bohr’s atomic model.

rubric.why: Bohr proposed that electrons move in particular allowed orbits around the nucleus.
rubric.description: States that electrons revolve around the nucleus in fixed orbits.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the fixed-orbit postulate.

rubric.why: Each permitted orbit has a definite energy.
rubric.description: States that each orbit has a fixed, definite energy.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the energy-level postulate.

rubric.why: Electrons in allowed stationary orbits do not continuously lose energy.
rubric.description: States that electrons do not emit energy while in an allowed orbit.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the no-radiation postulate.

rubric.why: Energy is exchanged when an electron changes between permitted orbits.
rubric.description: States that an electron absorbs or emits energy when it jumps between energy levels.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the transition-and-energy postulate.

rubric.why: Bohr’s quantization condition restricts the electron’s allowed angular momentum.
rubric.description: Gives the quantized angular momentum condition.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for mvr = nh/2π, or an equivalent statement of quantized angular momentum.

modelAnswer: Electrons revolve around the nucleus in certain fixed circular orbits, also called stationary orbits.
Each permitted orbit has a definite energy.
An electron does not radiate energy while it remains in an allowed stationary orbit.
An electron absorbs or emits energy only when it jumps between orbits; the energy change equals the difference between the two energy levels.
The angular momentum of an electron in an allowed orbit is quantized: mvr = nh/2π, where n is a whole number.

items.followUp: Write four differences between an atom and an atomic ion.

rubric.why: A molecule has no overall electrical charge.
rubric.description: States that a molecule is electrically neutral.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the neutral nature of a molecule.

rubric.why: A molecular ion has an overall positive or negative charge.
rubric.description: States that a molecular ion carries a net charge.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the charged nature of a molecular ion.

accept: equal number of protons and electrons
rubric.why: Equal proton and electron numbers account for a molecule’s zero net charge.
rubric.description: Distinguishes molecules by equal numbers of protons and electrons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct particle-count distinction.

accept: unequal number of protons and electrons
rubric.why: A valid example or the unequal proton/electron count distinguishes molecular ions.
rubric.description: Gives a correct molecular-ion example or states that its proton and electron numbers are unequal.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a suitable example, such as NH₄⁺ or SO₄²⁻, or the correct particle-count distinction.

modelAnswer: A molecule is a group of chemically bonded atoms with no net electrical charge; a molecular ion is a bonded group of atoms with a net charge.
A molecule has equal numbers of protons and electrons; a molecular ion has unequal numbers of protons and electrons.
A molecule is written without an overall charge, whereas a molecular ion is written with its charge as a superscript.
Examples: H₂O is a molecule; NH₄⁺ is a molecular ion.
